title: Kimchi Jjigae
subtitle: Korean kimchi stew with pork and tofu
excerpt: Kimchi jjigae is the most iconic Korean stew: aged kimchi simmered with pork belly, tofu, and gochugaru in a deeply flavoured broth. Old, sour kimchi (well-fermented, with a strong tang) is preferred; the fermented funk drives the flavour of the broth. This is a 30-minute weeknight dish that improves on reheating.
sourceNotes: Kimchi jjigae is considered the most representative dish of Korean home cooking. The stew has no fixed recipe: it uses whatever protein is available (pork, tuna, spam, or tofu alone for vegetarians) with sour kimchi as the primary ingredient. The kimchi should be well-fermented. Grocery store kimchi that has been in the jar for several weeks is ideal.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Kimchi jjigae tastes better the next day. Refrigerate and reheat gently.

content.text: Use the sourest, most fermented kimchi you can find, not fresh kimchi. The acid and funk from well-fermented kimchi is the defining flavour. Pour in the brine from the kimchi jar: it is the most flavourful liquid in the dish. The tofu goes in at the end so it holds its shape.

items.prepNote: well-fermented, cut into bite-sized pieces, brine reserved

content.text: Cook the pork belly in a dry pot over medium-high heat for 4 to 5 minutes until lightly browned. No oil needed: the pork fat renders as it heats.
Add the kimchi and the reserved brine. Stir in the gochugaru, gochujang, soy sauce, and garlic. Pour in 600 ml of water. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 20 minutes.

Add the tofu. Simmer gently for 5 more minutes. Do not stir vigorously or the tofu will break apart. Drizzle with sesame oil. Serve in the pot at the table with bowls of steamed rice and spring onion scattered over.

items.symptom: Stew lacks depth and tastes flat
items.cause: Kimchi was too fresh or the brine was not used
items.fix: Fresh kimchi lacks the fermented complexity of aged kimchi. If your kimchi is young, simmer it longer (up to 40 minutes) to develop the flavour. Always add the brine.
